title: Data Maker: Airport Route Survey
text:
This notebook creates fictional data. None of the respondents are real.
The imagined scenario: the airport commissioned a survey of travelers who live in the Southwestern part of the Madison, Wisconsin metropolitan area. The survey asked two questions:

Which route do you usually take to the airport?

North: around the top of Lake Mendota
Isthmus: straight through downtown on the isthmus
South: east on the Beltline, then north to the airport

Where are you from?

Madison native: raised in Madison
Greater Madison native: raised in the greater Madison area
Transplant: raised somewhere else, moved to Madison for work or other reasons


The research question is whether the route people take to the airport is related to whether or not they are from Madison.
Because we are making the data ourselves, we get to decide the answer ahead of time. That lets us later check whether a chi-square test finds the relationship we planted.

title: Using Python To Conduct Chi2 Analyses
text:
Welcome. This site is a collection of notes, examples, and walkthroughs for conducting chi-square (Chi2) analyses in Python.
Chi-square tests are one of the most common tools for asking whether two categorical variables are related. The notes here focus on the practical side: preparing data, running the test, and interpreting the results.

title: Using Python To Conduct Chi2 Analyses
text:
Site contents
A quick tour of the pages available from the navigation bar above.

Data Maker: data-maker.qmd
Generates a small, fictional survey dataset used elsewhere on the site. The scenario is an airport survey of Southwestern Madison travelers, recording each respondent’s origin and their usual route to the airport. Running this page writes airport_route_survey.csv next to the notebook so downstream pages have data to work with.


Data Preview: data-preview.qmd
A companion to Data Maker. Loads airport_route_survey.csv with pandas and prints the full dataset as a paginated, captioned table using Quarto’s df-print: paged option. Useful for confirming that the data generator produced what you expected.


Chi-Square Tutorial Airport Routes: chi2-example-tutorial-airport.qmd
A self-paced walkthrough of the chi-square test of independence, using the fictional data produced and previewed above. Covers hypotheses, expected values, normalized errors, degrees of freedom, and how to turn a chi-square statistic into a p-value. Tables and equations are numbered and cross-referenced, and the page ends with a scipy-generated reference table of chi-square critical values.


Chi-Square Tutorial Airport Routes in Python: chi2-example-tutorial-airport-python.qmd
The Python companion to the airport routes tutorial. Loads airport_route_survey.csv and carries out the same chi-square test using only base Python, pandas, numpy, and stats.chi2.sf(). Each step (expected values, errors, squared errors, normalized squared errors, the chi-square statistic, and the p-value) is built three ways: cell by cell, with for loops, and with matrix operations.


Chi-Square Tutorial Airport Routes, Pragmatic: chi2-example-tutorial-airport-pragmatic.qmd
The everyday version of the same analysis. Passes the observed counts to scipy.stats.chi2_contingency(), then checks assumptions, inspects standardized residuals, reports Cramér’s V as an effect size, wraps the workflow in a reusable function, and shows how to write up the result.


Chi-Square Tutorial Math Programs: chi2-example-tutorial-math.qmd
A self-paced walkthrough of the chi-square test of independence, using a fictional evaluation of three math programs. Covers hypotheses, expected values, normalized errors, degrees of freedom, and how to turn a chi-square statistic into a p-value. Tables and equations are numbered and cross-referenced, and the page ends with a scipy-generated reference table of chi-square critical values.

This is the third page in a series that runs one analysis three ways, all on the same data (airport_route_survey.csv, from the Data Maker page):

Check the assumptions
The chi-square test is an approximation, and it works well only under some conditions. Before trusting the p-value, check:

Two categorical variables. Yes: origin and route.
Independent observations. Each respondent appears once and answers once. (This is a matter of study design, not something code can check.)
Adequate expected counts. A common rule of thumb is that every expected count should be at least 5.

The third condition is easy to check because the function already returned the expected values. We wrap them in a DataFrame with the same labels as the observed table.

Which cells drive the result?
A significant chi-square statistic says something differs from independence, not what. To find out, look at the standardized (Pearson) residuals:
\[
\text{residual} = \frac{Observed - Expected}{\sqrt{Expected}}
\tag{1}\]
Residuals beyond about ±2 stand out, since values in that range would be unusual under independence. The sign tells you the direction: positive means more than expected, negative means fewer. Squaring each residual gives the normalized squared errors from the earlier lessons, so these are the same building blocks.

text:
How big is the effect?
With a large enough sample, even a tiny departure from independence is “significant.” So a p-value alone does not tell you whether a relationship matters in practice. An effect size can give more nuance to the interpretation. For chi-square tests, a standard choice is Cramér’s V:
\[
V = \sqrt{\frac{\chi^2}{n \times \min(rows - 1,\ columns - 1)}}
\tag{2}\]
V runs from 0 (no association) to 1 (perfect association).

n = observed.to_numpy().sum()
k = min(observed.shape) - 1

cramers_v = np.sqrt(result.statistic / (n * k))
print(f"Cramér's V: {cramers_v:.3f}")

text:
Wrap it in a function
Once you have done the analysis a few times, put the routine parts in a function so that any pair of categorical columns can be tested with one call.

def chi2_report(data, row_var, col_var, row_order=None, col_order=None):
    """Run a chi-square test of independence on two categorical columns."""
    table = pd.crosstab(data[row_var], data[col_var])
    if row_order is not None:
        table = table.loc[row_order]
    if col_order is not None:
        table = table[col_order]

    res = chi2_contingency(table)
    expected = pd.DataFrame(
        res.expected_freq, index=table.index, 
        columns=table.columns)

    n = table.to_numpy().sum()
    v = np.sqrt(res.statistic / (n * (min(table.shape) - 1)))

    return {
        "observed": table,
        "expected": expected,
        "residuals": (table - expected) / np.sqrt(expected),
        "chi2": res.statistic,
        "dof": res.dof,
        "n": n,
        "p": res.pvalue,
        "cramers_v": v,
        "min_expected": expected.to_numpy().min(),
    }


report = chi2_report(survey, "origin", "route", origins, routes)

print(f"chi2({report['dof']}, N = {report['n']}) = {report['chi2']:.2f}, "
      f"p = {report['p']:.2e}, V = {report['cramers_v']:.2f}")

chi2(4, N = 300) = 42.25, p = 1.48e-08, V = 0.27


Because the function takes column names as arguments, we can reuse it immediately on a different question. Here we check the survey against itself with the roles of the variables swapped. The chi-square statistic is symmetric, so the answer is the same.

swapped = chi2_report(survey, "route", "origin", routes, origins)

print(f"chi2({swapped['dof']}, N = {swapped['n']}) = {swapped['chi2']:.2f}, "
      f"p = {swapped['p']:.2e}, V = {swapped['cramers_v']:.2f}")

text:
Make the decision and write it up
The decision rule is the same as before: If the p-value is below the significance level (conventionally 0.05), reject the null hypothesis.

alpha = 0.05
print("Reject H0" if report["p"] < alpha else "Fail to reject H0")

Reject H0


A typical write-up for a report or manuscript states the statistic, the degrees of freedom, the sample size, the p-value, and the effect size:

A chi-square test of independence found a significant association between where travelers are from and the route they take to the airport, \(\chi^2\)(4, N = 300) = 42.25, p < .001, Cramér’s V = 0.27. Madison natives took the Isthmus route more often than expected, and Greater Madison natives took the South route more often than expected.







What this does and does not tell you



Rejecting the null hypothesis tells us the two variables are related. It does not show that where a person is from causes their route choice, and it says nothing beyond the population that was sampled. Remember also that the data here are fictional, and the Data Maker page deliberately built the relationship into them.

        m (list): A list of lists containing numerical values (ints or floats).

            - 'sum_of_cells' (int or float): Total sum of all numerical values.

            - 'max_index' (tuple): Coordinates (row, column) of the largest value.

        'sum_of_cells': 0,
        'max_value': m[0][0],
        'min_value': m[0][0],
        'max_index': (0, 0),

            # print(f"{m[row][col]} - ")
            ret_dict['total_cells'] += 1
            ret_dict['sum_of_cells'] += m[row][col]
            if m[row][col] > ret_dict['max_value']:

            if m[row][col] < ret_dict['min_value']:

                ret_dict['min_index'] = (row, col)

    ret_dict['avgerage_of_cells'] = \
        ret_dict['sum_of_cells'] / ret_dict['total_cells']

    if verbose:

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence: A Worked Example (Airport Routes)
text:
The big idea
Sometimes we want to know whether two categorical variables are related. A categorical variable is one whose values are categories rather than numbers, like a favorite color, a type of program, or a choice of route.






Refresher: what is a categorical variable?



A categorical variable records which group an observation belongs to. You will also see these called nominal variables. The two terms are effectively interchangeable in scientific use. When the categories have a natural order (small, medium, large) some texts split them off as ordinal.
Examples of categorical / nominal variables:

Favorite color: red, blue, green
Route to the airport: North, Isthmus, South
Where a person is from: Madison native, Greater Madison native, Transplant
Post-high-school outcome: work, tech school, college, military

The chi-square test of independence expects two categorical variables. If one of your variables is a count or a continuous measurement, you would usually reach for a different tool (a t-test, ANOVA, correlation, or regression, depending on the question).


The chi-square test of independence (chi rhymes with sky) helps us decide between two possibilities:

The two variables are independent: Knowing one cannot help you predict the other.
The two variables are dependent: Knowing one can help you predict the other.

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence: A Worked Example (Airport Routes)
text:
The scenario
Imagine the airport commissioned a survey of travelers who live in the Southwestern part of the Madison, Wisconsin metropolitan area. (The data are fictional. They were created on the Data Maker page and can be previewed on the Data Preview page.) The survey asked each respondent two questions.
Which route do you usually take to the airport?

North: around the top of Lake Mendota
Isthmus: straight through downtown on the isthmus
South: east on the Beltline, then north to the airport

Where are you from?

Madison native
Greater Madison native
Transplant: raised somewhere else, moved to Madison for work or other reasons

Every respondent gave exactly one answer to each question. There were 300 respondents in total.
Research question: Does the route people take to the airport relate to where they are from?

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence: A Worked Example (Airport Routes)
text:
The hypotheses
Every statistical test begins with two competing statements called hypotheses.

Null hypothesis: There is no relationship. The route a traveler takes to the airport is independent of where the traveler is from.
Alternative hypothesis: There is a relationship. The route a traveler takes to the airport depends on where the traveler is from.

The test works by assuming the null hypothesis is true, and then asking how surprising our data would be if that were so. If the data would be very surprising, we reject the null hypothesis.

A word about matrices

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence: A Worked Example (Airport Routes)
text:
The formula
Here is the formula for the chi-square statistic, which is often written as χ² or X²:
\[
\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{(Observed_i - Expected_i)^2}{Expected_i}
\tag{1}\]
In plain words, for each cell:

Subtract the expected values (the values you will calculate from the observed data) from the observed value (the actual values in the observed table).
Square that difference (the differences between observed and expected are known as the errors).
Divide by the expected value for that cell.

Then add up the results from every cell. The symbol Σ (sigma) means “add up,” and the little i simply means “for each cell, one at a time.”
You already have the observed values. The next step is to find the expected values.

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence: A Worked Example (Airport Routes)
text:
Step 1: Calculate the expected values

What is an expected value?
An expected value answers this question: If the null hypothesis were true and there were no relationship, how many respondents would we expect to see in this cell? The expected value tells us what the counts would be if where a person is from made no difference to the route they take.
If origin made no difference, then each origin group would use each route in the same proportions as the group overall. The expected values capture exactly that.


The recipe
For each cell:
\[
Expected = \frac{Row\ Total \times Column\ Total}{Grand\ Total}
\tag{2}\]

Step 2: Calculate the normalized errors
Next, compare each observed value with its expected value. For each cell, calculate:
\[
\frac{(Observed - Expected)^2}{Expected}
\tag{5}\]
This quantity is sometimes called a normalized error. The difference (observed minus expected) is the error. Squaring it makes every error positive, so errors in opposite directions cannot cancel each other out. Dividing by the expected value puts each error in proportion to the size of its cell.
Notice that the expected matrix is used twice here: Once to find the difference, and again to divide.

Worked example: Madison native, North

Observed: 18 (from Table 1)
Expected: 14.80 (from Table 4)

\[
\frac{(18 - 14.8)^2}{14.8} = \frac{(3.2)^2}{14.8} = \frac{10.24}{14.8} = 0.692
\tag{6}\]


A second example: Greater Madison native, Isthmus
\[
\frac{(12 - 25.68)^2}{25.68} = \frac{(-13.68)^2}{25.68} = \frac{187.142}{25.68} = 7.287
\tag{7}\]
Here the difference was negative, but squaring it made the result positive.

section: Step 3: Add them up to get the chi-square statistic
text:
Step 3: Add them up to get the chi-square statistic
The chi-square statistic is the sum of all the normalized errors:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\chi^2 &= 0.692 + 12.685 + 11.586 \\
       &\quad + 0.037 + 7.287 + 5.553 \\
       &\quad + 0.433 + 1.826 + 2.151
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}\]
\[
\chi^2 = 42.2522
\tag{9}\]
That’s it. A few simple operations, repeated across the matrix, give us our chi-square statistic. This chi-square statistic is the statistic you will want to report in your manuscript, report, or results. You’ll also want to report the degrees of freedom (discussed below). Ultimately you’ll need this chi-square statistic in addition to the degrees of freedom to find the p-value, which is what will inform your decision on whether to reject (or fail to reject) the null hypothesis. Typically, you will also report the p-value when reporting your results.






Rounding



If you add the rounded values above, you get 42.250. The value 42.2522 comes from carrying all the decimal places through each step. Small differences in the last decimal place are normal and do not change the conclusion.

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence: A Worked Example (Airport Routes)
section: Step 4: Find the degrees of freedom
text:
Step 4: Find the degrees of freedom
To turn the chi-square statistic into a p-value, we need one more number, called the degrees of freedom (often written as df). For a chi-square test of independence:
\[
df = (\text{number of rows} - 1) \times (\text{number of columns} - 1)
\tag{10}\]
Count only the rows and columns of categories, not the totals. Our table has 3 origins and 3 routes:
\[
df = (3 - 1) \times (3 - 1) = 2 \times 2 = 4
\tag{11}\]

section: Step 5: Find the p-value and make a decision
text:
Step 5: Find the p-value and make a decision

What a p-value tells you
The p-value is the probability of getting results as extreme as ours, or more extreme, if the null hypothesis were true. A small p-value means our data would be surprising in a world with no relationship.
We compare the p-value to a cutoff called the significance level. The conventional significance level is 0.05.

If the p-value is less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude there is a relationship.
If the p-value is 0.05 or greater, we fail to reject the null hypothesis. We do not have enough evidence of a relationship.



Using the table
The chi-square reference table (Table 10) at the end of this lesson lets you estimate the p-value. It is a right-tailed table: the column headings are p-values, and the numbers inside the table are chi-square statistics. Bigger chi-square statistics sit farther to the right, where the p-values are smaller.
To use it:

Find the row that matches your degrees of freedom.
Move across that row until you find where your chi-square statistic fits between two numbers.
Read the p-values at the top of those two columns. Your p-value lies between them.

Now walk through how to read this, one step at a time:

Find the right row. Our test has 4 degrees of freedom, so every comparison happens along the circled row (ignore the rows for 3 and 5). We show these additional rows here only so you can see the pattern of critical values rising with df.
Scan left to right along that row. The numbers in the row are the chi-square statistic you would need to reach to hit each p-value at the top of the table. As you move right, the p-values shrink (0.995 down to 0.005), and the critical values grow.
Place your own chi-square statistic among them. Our statistic is 42.2522. Compare this value to each critical value in the row. It’s bigger than 13.277 (the value under the 0.01 column), and it’s also bigger than 14.860 (the value under the circled 0.005 column).
Notice it’s bigger than every value in the row. Because 42.2522 exceeds even the critical value in the smallest p-value column the table shows (0.005), our result is more extreme than anything this row directly reports.
Translate that into a p-value. A chi-square statistic that clears the 0.005 column’s critical value means the true p-value is smaller than 0.005. This is as precise as the printed table alone can get you. It tells you a ceiling (p < 0.005), not an exact number.
Confirm with the exact value. Software can compute the precise p-value instead of just bounding it. Here, the exact p-value is about 0.000000015 (1.5 × 10⁻⁸), which is indeed smaller than 0.005 (consistent with what the table told us).







Finding exact p-values before software



Today, getting an exact p-value is one function call away. That convenience is fairly new. For most of the history of this test, researchers had no computer to ask, so they relied on printed tables like the one above.
Someone, working by hand or with an early mechanical calculator, had to work out the chi-square distribution’s shape for every degree of freedom and figure out exactly which value cut off the top 0.005 (or 0.05, or 0.10) of that distribution’s area. That’s a calculus problem, not an arithmetic problem, and it isn’t something you can do quickly with pencil and paper for even one value, let alone hundreds. So statisticians did that hard work once, wrote the answers down in reference tables like this one, and everyone else just looked up their result the same way you might look up a word in a dictionary rather than working out its definition from scratch every time.
That’s also why these tables only show a handful of columns like 0.10, 0.05, 0.025, and 0.005, instead of every possible p-value. If your chi-square statistic landed between two columns, or beyond the last one like ours did, the most honest answer available to a researcher in, say, 1950 was a range: “somewhere less than 0.005,” not an exact figure.
This is part of why the reject/fail-to-reject language exists at all. Historically, decisions were built around comparing a calculated statistic to a small handful of tabulated thresholds, not around reading off one precise, always-available number. Today, software has just replaced the physical page and closed the gap between columns.


Decision: The p-value is less than 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis. There is evidence in favor of believing that there is a relationship between where travelers are from and the route they take to the airport. We have not proven that there is a relationship. We have not proven that being from a certain place causes a traveler to choose a certain route. Merely we have rejected the null hypothesis that there is no relationship, which then means we would tend to believe the alternative hypothesis.
Reminder on the null and alternative hypotheses:

Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): There is no relationship between where travelers are from and the route they take to the airport.
Alternative hypothesis (\(H_1\)): There is a relationship between where travelers are from and the route they take to the airport.

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence: A Worked Example (Airport Routes)
text:
Interpreting the two analyses together
Both analyses led to the same decision, but the evidence was much stronger when we kept the three origin groups separate (p about 0.000000015) than when we combined the two native groups (p about 0.027). Combining categories threw away information: Madison natives and Greater Madison natives behave differently from each other, and lumping them together blurred that difference.
Keep in mind, too, that a chi-square test tells you whether two variables are related. It does not, on its own, tell you that one variable caused the other. It also does not tell you which cells drive the result. The normalized errors help with that, because they point to the cells that contribute the most.
Remember also that the data here are fictional, and that we built the relationship into the data ourselves on the Data Maker page. In real survey work you would also want to think about how respondents were selected, since a sample that is not representative of travelers can distort the results.

section: Other ways to get the p-value
text:
Other ways to get the p-value
The table gives you a range. Software can give you the exact p-value. In Excel, there are two functions for this.
Excel’s function CHISQ.TEST() compares the observed values with the expected values and returns the p-value directly. You give it the observed range first and the expected range second:
=CHISQ.TEST(observed range, expected range)
Excel’s function CHISQ.DIST.RT() converts a chi-square statistic into a p-value. You give it the chi-square statistic and the degrees of freedom:
=CHISQ.DIST.RT(chi-square statistic, degrees of freedom)
For the combined-natives table, =CHISQ.DIST.RT(7.2311, 2) returns 0.027.
In upcoming tutorials, you will learn to carry out this same analysis in Python. Every step you did by hand here, from the expected values to the final p-value, has a direct counterpart in code.
There are also websites that will find the p-value for free if you know the chi2 and df statistics.

Row total: (right-hand column) is the number of students in one math program.
Column total: (bottom row) is the number of students with one outcome.
Grand total: (bottom-right corner) is the number of students overall.

The counts in the table, the numbers we actually saw, are called the observed values.






A word about matrices



A grid of numbers arranged in rows and columns is called a matrix (sounds fancier than it is). The core of each table above, without the totals, is a matrix with 3 rows and 4 columns. In this lesson you will build two more matrices of the same size. Doing the same calculation “for every cell in the matrix” is a pattern you will see often, especially once we move to Python.

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence: A Worked Example (Math Program Evaluation)
text:
The formula
Here is the formula for the chi-square statistic, which is often written as χ² or X²:
\[
\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{(Observed_i - Expected_i)^2}{Expected_i}
\tag{1}\]
In plain words, for each cell:

Subtract the expected values (the values you will calculate from the observed data) from the observed value (the actual values in the observed table).
Square that difference (the differences between observed and expected are known as the errors).
Divide by the expected value for that cell.

Then add up the results from every cell. The symbol Σ (sigma) means “add up,” and the little i simply means “for each cell, one at a time.”
You already have the observed values. The next step is to find the expected values.

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence: A Worked Example (Math Program Evaluation)
text:
Step 1: Calculate the expected values

What is an expected value?
An expected value answers this question: If the null hypothesis were true and there were no relationship, how many students would we expect to see in this cell? The expected value tells us what the counts would be if the math program made no difference.
If the math program made no difference, then each program would send students to each outcome in the same proportions as the group overall. The expected values capture exactly that.


The recipe
For each cell:
\[
Expected = \frac{Row\ Total \times Column\ Total}{Grand\ Total}
\tag{2}\]

Step 2: Calculate the normalized errors

text:
Step 3: Add them up to get the chi-square statistic
The chi-square statistic is the sum of all the normalized errors:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\chi^2 &= 0.344 + 1.706 + 6.240 + 0.029 \\
       &\quad + 0.467 + 0.287 + 0.099 + 0.080 \\
       &\quad + 1.538 + 0.552 + 7.481 + 0.012
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}\]
\[
\chi^2 = 18.8346
\tag{9}\]
That’s it. A few simple operations, repeated across the matrix, give us our chi-square statistic. This chi-square statistic is the statistic you will want to report in your manuscript, report, or results. You’ll also want to report the degrees of freedom (discussed below). Ultimately you’ll need this chi-square staistics in addition to the degrees of freedom to find the p-value which is what will inform your decision on whether to reject (or fail to reject) the null hypothesis. Typically, you will also report the p-value when reporting your results.






Rounding



If you add the rounded values above, you get 18.835. The value 18.8346 comes from carrying all the decimal places through each step. Small differences in the last decimal place are normal and do not change the conclusion.

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence: A Worked Example (Math Program Evaluation)
section: Step 4: Find the degrees of freedom
text:
Step 4: Find the degrees of freedom
To turn the chi-square statistic into a p-value, we need one more number, called the degrees of freedom (often written as df). For a chi-square test of independence:
\[
df = (\text{number of rows} - 1) \times (\text{number of columns} - 1)
\tag{10}\]
Count only the rows and columns of categories, not the totals. Our table has 3 math programs and 4 outcomes:
\[
df = (3 - 1) \times (4 - 1) = 2 \times 3 = 6
\tag{11}\]

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence: A Worked Example (Math Program Evaluation)
section: Step 5: Find the p-value and make a decision
text:
Step 5: Find the p-value and make a decision

What a p-value tells you
The p-value is the probability of getting results as extreme as ours, or more extreme, if the null hypothesis were true. A small p-value means our data would be surprising in a world with no relationship.
We compare the p-value to a cutoff called the significance level. The conventional significance level is 0.05.

If the p-value is less than 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis and conclude there is a relationship.
If the p-value is 0.05 or greater, we fail to reject the null hypothesis. We do not have enough evidence of a relationship.



Using the table
The chi-square reference table (Table 11) at the end of this lesson lets you estimate the p-value. It is a right-tailed table: the column headings are p-values, and the numbers inside the table are chi-square statistics. Bigger chi-square statistics sit farther to the right, where the p-values are smaller.
To use it:

Find the row that matches your degrees of freedom.
Move across that row until you find where your chi-square statistic fits between two numbers.
Read the p-values at the top of those two columns. Your p-value lies between them.

Find the right row. Our test has 6 degrees of freedom, so every comparison happens along the circled row (ignore the rows for 4, 5, 7, and 8). We show these additional rows here only so you can see the pattern of critical values rising and falling with df.
Scan left to right along that row. The numbers in the row are the chi-square statistic you would need to reach to hit each p-value at the top of the table. As you move right, the p-values shrink (0.995 down to 0.005), and the critical values grow.
Place your own chi-square statistic among them. Our statistic is 18.8346. Compare this 18.8346 value to each critical value in the row. iIt’s bigger than 16.812 (the value under the 0.01 column), and it’s also bigger than 18.548 (the value under the circled 0.005 column).
Notice it’s bigger than every value shown in the row. Because 18.8346 exceeds even the critical value in the smallest p-value column this table excerpt shows (0.005), our result is more extreme than anything this row directly reports.
Translate that into a p-value. A chi-square statistic that clears the 0.005 column’s critical value means the true p-value is smaller than 0.005. This is as precise as the printed table alone can get you. The tells you a ceiling (p < 0.005), not an exact number.
Confirm with the exact value. Software can compute the precise p-value instead of just bounding it. Here, the exact p-value is 0.00445, which is indeed smaller than 0.005 (consistent with what the table told us).







Finding exact p-values before software



Today, getting an exact p-value is one function call away. That convenience is fairly new. For most of the history of this test, researchers had no computer to ask, so they relied on printed tables like the one above.
Someone, working by hand or with an early mechanical calculator, had to work out the chi-square distribution’s shape for every degree of freedom and figure out exactly which value cut off the top 0.005 (or 0.05, or 0.10) of that distribution’s area. That’s a calculus problem, not an arithmetic problem, and it isn’t something you can do quickly with pencil and paper for even one value, let alone hundreds. So statisticians did that hard work once, wrote the answers down in reference tables like this one, and everyone else just looked up their result the same way you might look up a word in a dictionary rather than working out its definition from scratch every time.
That’s also why these tables only show a handful of columns like 0.10, 0.05, 0.025, and 0.005, instead of every possible p-value. Each column had to be calculated and typeset by hand, so the table’s authors picked a small, useful set of round, commonly needed values and stopped there. If your chi-square statistic landed between two columns, or beyond the last one like ours did, the most honest answer available to a researcher in, say, 1950 was a range: “somewhere less than 0.005,” not “0.00445.” Getting the exact figure would have meant doing the underlying calculus yourself, which almost no one working on an applied research question would attempt today.
This is part of why the reject/fail-to-reject language exists at all. Historically, decisions were built around comparing a calculated statistic to a small handful of tabulated thresholds, not around reading off one precise, always-available number. The table you used above to conclude “p is less than 0.005” is doing the exact same job those printed pages did decades ago. Today, software has just replaced the physical page and closed the gap between columns.


Decision for year one: The p-value is less than 0.05, so we reject the null hypothesis. In year one, there is evidence in favor of believing that there is a relationship between the math program in which students participated and their post-high-school outcomes. We have not proven that there is a relationship. We have not proven that one math program influences student outcomes. Merely we have rejected the null hypothesis that there is no relationship, which then means we would tend to believe the alternate hypothesis.
Reminder on the null and alternative hypotheses:

Null hypothesis (\(H_0\)): There is no relationship between the math program in which students participated and their post-high-school outcomes.
Alternative hypothesis (\(H_1\)): There is a relationship between the math program in which students participated and their post-high-school outcomes.

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence: A Worked Example (Math Program Evaluation)
text:
Interpreting the two years together
The two years led to different conclusions. Year one showed evidence of a relationship, and year two did not. This is a useful reminder that one test on one set of data is not the final word. Results can differ from sample to sample, which is why repeating a study matters.
In a scenario such as this we might attribute the first year result as something that is known as an “implementation bump” or “implementation dip” which is a common result in observational field studies, and also in randomized controlled trial field studies where initial enthusiasm or novelty affects participation. Keep in mind, too, that a chi-square test tells you whether two variables are related. It does not, on its own, tell you that one variable caused the other.
Remember also that we set aside how students were placed into each program. If, for example, the selection mechanism related to the outcome then it would confound the results and make it difficult to determine the true effect of the program on post-high-school outcomes. This is why random assignment is so valuable when feasible.

section: Other ways to get the p-value
text:
Other ways to get the p-value
The table gives you a range. Software can give you the exact p-value. In Excel, there are two functions for this.
Excel’s function CHISQ.TEST() compares the observed values with the expected values and returns the p-value directly. You give it the observed range first and the expected range second:
=CHISQ.TEST(observed range, expected range)
Excel’s function CHISQ.DIST.RT() converts a chi-square statistic into a p-value. You give it the chi-square statistic and the degrees of freedom:
=CHISQ.DIST.RT(chi-square statistic, degrees of freedom)
For year one, =CHISQ.DIST.RT(18.8346, 6) returns 0.00445.
In upcoming tutorials, you will learn to carry out this same analysis in Python. Every step you did by hand here, from the expected values to the final p-value, has a direct counterpart in code.
There are also websites that will find the p-value for free if you know the chi2 and df statistics.

text:
Three ways to do the same thing
The rest of this lesson performs steps 2 through 7 three times, using three different styles of coding. All three produce identical answers. The point is to see how the same idea can be expressed more and more compactly.

Best for

B. For loops

Speed and brevity; how experienced analysts do it

Step 2: Expected values

Make the decision
The decision rule has not changed since the pencil-and-paper lesson. We compare the p-value to the significance level, conventionally 0.05.

alpha = 0.05

print(f"Chi-square statistic: {chi2_c:.4f}")
print(f"Degrees of freedom:   {df_c}")
print(f"p-value:              {p_value_c:.2e}")
print()

if p_value_c < alpha:
    print("Reject the null hypothesis: the data provide evidence that route depends on origin.")
else:
    print("Fail to reject the null hypothesis: no evidence that route depends on origin.")

Chi-square statistic: 42.2522
Degrees of freedom:   4
p-value:              1.48e-08

Reject the null hypothesis: the data provide evidence that route depends on origin.


Decision: With \(\chi^2\) = 42.2522, \(df\) = 4, and a p-value of about 1.5e-08, we reject the null hypothesis. There is evidence that the route travelers take to the airport is related to where they are from.






What this does and does not tell you



Rejecting the null hypothesis tells us the two variables are related. It does not prove that being from a certain place causes someone to choose a certain route, and it does not say which cells drive the result. The normalized errors help with that. Also remember the data here are fictional, and the Data Maker page deliberately built the relationship into them.

title: Chi-Square Test of Independence in Python (Airport Routes)
text:
Summary

Load the data with pd.read_csv() and build the cross tabulation with pd.crosstab().
Convert it to a numpy array with .to_numpy(). This is the observed matrix.
Find the row totals, column totals, and grand total with .sum().
Calculate the expected values: row total × column total ÷ grand total.
Calculate the errors: observed − expected.
Square the errors.
Divide the squared errors by the expected values to get the normalized squared errors.
Add up the normalized squared errors to get the chi-square statistic.
Find the degrees of freedom: (rows − 1) × (columns − 1).
Convert the chi-square statistic and degrees of freedom to a p-value with stats.chi2.sf().
If the p-value is less than 0.05, reject the null hypothesis. Otherwise, fail to reject it.

Steps 4 through 8 can be written cell by cell, with nested for loops, or as matrix operations. All three give the same answer.
